The timeline, scope and blast radius are solidly established and unchanged from round 1: a single-minute step in auth-service error_rate from ~0.2% to ~36% at 14:02:00Z, flat throughput (~400 req/s) and p99 (~90ms), a flat ~2h plateau (F8/F17/F28), a contemporaneous ~21% plateau at api-gateway (F11), and a fleet-wide sweep showing the only changes all day are auth-service dep-5710 (14:00Z, jjwt 0.11→0.12 "breaking parser API", TokenValidator rewritten) and cfg-2705 (14:01Z, jwt.signing.key_id k-2025-10→k-2026-04). Both precede the 14:02Z onset by 1–2 minutes. That localization is trustworthy and kills H3, H4 (resource arm) and H5.

The problem is that H1 (code regression) and H2 (key rotation) are still TIED (0.50 vs 0.42) and name different origins and different fixes, and round 2 produced essentially no new discriminating evidence — it mostly confirmed what was already known. Round 2's T4/T5/T6 returned negative results (no pod/endpoint/issuer label exists; change metadata has no diff, no key-rotation mode, no JWKS-source field), so the decisive tests my round-1 review named are now shown to be unreachable through change/observability metadata, NOT merely unrequested. Only one discriminating line remains open and it is cheap: the confirmatory rollback/revert of one of the two changes. Meanwhile H2 has an internal weakness the team itself flagged and never resolved (a flat 2h plateau is a poor fit for a propagation race unless reload is permanently stalled) and H1's mechanism hop ("rewritten validator inverts a token class") is still completely unevidenced (F34: no diff; F16/F33: the deployed jjwt version is self-contradictory so we don't even know what parser semantics changed). Neither leader is adequately proven; I cannot accept either, and I still do not call inconclusive because one decisive, obtainable falsification test exists.

Two additional quality issues: (a) F31 shows the "restarts" metric query and the auth-service ERROR log query both failed (503), so the pod-restart arm of H4 is NOT closed out as the reasoning claims; the flat cpu/memory (F29) argues against resource pressure but not against a crash-looping subset. (b) The 36% figure is being read as a "deterministic class cut" but it is a service aggregate with no issuer/instance dimension (F26), so the "~1/3 of tokens" framing is an inference from one number, not a measured partition — it cannot be used to favor H1 over H2. The team's rejection of H5 also leans on "internally consistent" metrics while the identity-namespace log pipeline is down; that is acceptable but only because the caller-side 21% plateau (F11) is an independent series.

challenges.issue: Mechanism hop is entirely unevidenced and may be unevidenced-in-principle from available data: F34 shows the TokenValidator rewrite is only the string 'TokenValidator rewritten' (no diff, no clock-skew/strictness defaults), and F16/F33 show the deploy metadata is self-contradictory ('JWT library to 4.x' vs 'jjwt 0.11 -> 0.12'). We therefore do not know what parser semantics changed, yet the whole hypothesis rests on 'the new validator inverts valid tokens'. H1 currently wins on timing fit and a historic precedent (HIST-109) that the team itself labels a lead only. Accepted as a real candidate, not as proven.

The propagation mechanism is contradicted by the data the team collected: a key-id-propagation race should converge as pods reload, but the error is a flat 35–39% plateau for ~2h with no decay (F8/F17/F28). Explaining this requires an unobserved 'stalled reload' that no finding supports. Also, F35 shows the config record has no dual-key/grace-period/reload fields either way, so hard-cutover-vs-staged is untested, not established. H2 is viable mainly because HIST-108 matches the symptom class, which is a lead, not evidence.

No evidence partitions the failures by token-issuance epoch or key_id relative to 14:01Z. H2's distinctive prediction (failures defined by which key the token/validator used) is unmeasured; the 36% figure is a single fleet-aggregate number (F26), so citing it as a '~1/3 subset' for H2's mechanism is inference, not measurement.

Not actually closed out as the ranking claims: F31 and the tool-reliability log show the 'restarts' metric (correct name) and the auth-service ERROR log query both failed with backend 503, so pod restart counts are unknown. F29 (flat cpu/memory) argues against resource pressure but does not exclude a crash-looping/hung subset of pods. H4 is low-probability but not eliminated.

H1 is asserted to predict a cut that is 'uniform across instances', but no instance-level data exists (F26) and the request for it will not succeed; the team has effectively converted an unmeasurable test into an assumption. This should be an explicit, stated assumption driving the confidence cap rather than an implicit support.

H5 was rejected partly on 'metrics are internally consistent' while the metrics backend is the same backend whose namespace log pipeline is down and whose restart/log queries return 503. The rejection survives only because the caller-side api-gateway series (F11) is an independent observation of the same incident window — worth stating explicitly rather than relying on metric self-consistency.

evidence_requests.question: Was either change rolled back or reverted at any point between now and the last queries — i.e. re-check get_deployments and get_config_changes for auth-service dep-5710 (rolled_back_at) and cfg-2705 (any revert/re-publish of the previous key_id k-2025-10), and for any rollback event in the fleet after 14:00Z. If a single-change rollback experiment has been run or is runnable (roll back dep-5710 only, or revert cfg-2705 only), report which one was reverted and the auth-service error_rate in the minutes immediately after.
evidence_requests.rationale: This is the single decisive falsification test that separates H1 from H2: reverting only cfg-2705 and seeing error_rate return to ~0.2% proves H2; reverting only dep-5710 and seeing recovery proves H1. Both changes are still 'live' with rolled_back_at null (F13/F14/F32), so this is untested and it is the only discriminating evidence shown to be obtainable — the per-instance/per-issuer and change-diff routes are now confirmed unavailable.

evidence_requests.question: Does any data source — change metadata, config store, dependency graph, or incident history — expose the JWKS/key-loading model for auth-service: does it read the signing key from a single shared source (so all pods switch atomically) or from per-pod JWKS with independent reload? And is there any record (including prior-incident resolution notes, e.g. HIST-108's fix of re-publishing the previous key) of whether cfg-2705 was a hard single-key swap or retained the previous key? If no field exists anywhere, say so explicitly.
evidence_requests.rationale: H2's only viable mechanism requires per-pod/stale-key loading; if auth-service reads one shared key source, the partial-propagation mechanism is impossible and H2 should be demoted below H1. Round-2 T5/T6 could not resolve this from cfg-2705's own record (F35), so I want confirmation that no other source (dependency graph attributes, historic-incident resolutions) carries it before treating it as permanently unavailable.

evidence_requests.question: Retry the two queries that failed with backend 503: auth-service metric 'restarts' and auth-service ERROR-level logs for 13:50Z–15:59Z. If either now succeeds, report restart counts across the onset and any 401/invalid_token error text, pod names, or key_id/issuer references. If the same 503 recurs (or the identity-namespace pipeline remains down per the incident note), report that these are permanently unavailable and stop retrying.
evidence_requests.rationale: The restart series is the one piece of evidence that would close out H4's pod-level arm (currently not eliminated — F31), and log text would confirm whether the failures are 'invalid_token' from a key mismatch (H2) versus a parser/claim rejection (H1). These failed only on backend 503, not on a known-permanent outage, so one bounded retry is worth it; the log pipeline note suggests the log half may be unavailable, in which case we stop.

critiques.summary:
Timeline, scope and blast radius are solid and unchanged across three rounds: a single-minute step in auth-service error_rate from ~0.2% to ~36% at 14:02:00Z, flat throughput (~400 req/s) and p99 (~90 ms), a flat ~2h plateau, a contemporaneous ~21% plateau at the unchanged caller api-gateway, and a fleet-wide sweep showing the only changes all day are auth-service dep-5710 (14:00Z, jjwt 0.11→0.12 'breaking parser API', TokenValidator rewritten) and cfg-2705 (14:01Z, jwt.signing.key_id k-2025-10→k-2026-04). That localization is trustworthy and eliminates H3 (clock/cert: no evidence, incoherent timing), H4's resource arm (F29/F30 flat CPU/memory/rate-limit) and H5 (api-gateway's independent, time-aligned plateau F11 is not a log-pipeline artifact).

What cannot be resolved is WHICH of the two auth-service changes caused it. H1 (code regression) and H2 (key rotation) name different origins and different fixes, and every discriminating test is now shown to be unreachable rather than merely unrequested: round 2 established there is no per-instance/pod, endpoint or token-issuer dimension (F26) so a uniform-vs-split partition cannot be measured; no metadata source exposes the TokenValidator diff, the deployed jjwt version (F33 contradictory) or clock-skew/claim-strictness defaults (F34); and no source anywhere exposes the key-loading topology or whether cfg-2705 was a hard swap or retained the previous key (F35/F43/F45/F47). Round 3's decisive test — a single-change rollback — is untested and unrunnable: dep-5710 rolled_back_at is null and cfg-2705 was never reverted anywhere in the fleet (F38/F39/F40/F41/F42), and the tooling is read-only. Logs are unavailable (identity-namespace pipeline down) so the error-string test (signature/unknown-key → H2 vs expiry/claim-parse → H1) is also impossible. Both surviving hypotheses consequently retain exactly one unevidenced mechanism hop; neither is confirmed nor excluded. Since the decisive evidence sources are permanently unavailable in this run, further querying would not help, so 'inconclusive' — not 'needs_evidence' — is the honest outcome. Practical note: H1 is the marginally better fit on shape (a flat 2h plateau with no decay fits a deterministic code/config fault better than a propagation race that should converge), so an operator forced to act should roll back dep-5710 first; but that is a shape argument, not proof, and I will not defend dep-5710 as the established root cause.

Secondary quality issues: the '~1/3 of tokens fail' framing is an inference from one aggregate number, not a measured partition (F26) and must not be used as evidence for either hypothesis; the pod-restart arm of H4 is NOT closed out (F31: 'restarts' metric and auth-service ERROR log queries both 503), though flat CPU/memory argues against resource pressure; and 'healthy metrics' claims rest on single series with a failing backend, so they should be read as 'no evidence of load/resource cause' rather than 'excluded'.

challenges.issue: Decisive mechanism hop is unevidenced: 'the rewritten validator inverts a class of valid tokens' has no support — no diff, no config values (F34), and the deployed jjwt version is self-contradictory (F33: 'JWT library to 4.x' vs 'jjwt 0.11 -> 0.12'), so we do not even know what parser semantics changed. The claim rests entirely on timing-and-shape (flat 2h plateau), which is a heuristic, not a mechanism.

Its one discriminating test was never run and is not runnable: rolling back dep-5710 alone would prove H1, but the deploy is still live (rolled_back_at null, F38) and the tooling is read-only. Without it, H1 and H2 remain strictly unseparated.

Same blocking gap from the other side: no source anywhere (cfg-2705 record, config store F43/F44, dependency graph F45/F47) states whether auth-service reads the signing key from one shared source or per-pod JWKS, and none states whether the rotation retained the previous key. H2's required mechanism is neither confirmable nor excludable from available evidence.

Internal shape weakness the team concedes: a key-propagation race should converge as validators reload, yet the error is a flat 35–39% plateau for ~2h with zero decay (F8/F17/F28/F27), requiring an unobserved permanently-stalled reload that no finding supports.

The '~1/3 of tokens fail' quantification is inferred from a single fleet-aggregate series with no issuer/instance/key dimension (F26). It is used rhetorically in both H1's and H2's favour and should be discarded as a partition, not cited as evidence.

The pod-restart arm was claimed closed by flat CPU/memory, but the discriminator is absent: 'restarts' metric and auth-service ERROR logs both failed 503 (F31) and no pod dimension exists (F26). Flat cpu/memory argues against resource pressure, not against a crash-looping or unmigrated subset.
Effectively unfalsifiable in this environment (no instance label), so it cannot be ranked against H1/H2 by evidence — it should be carried as an unresolved low-probability unknown rather than scored.

Correctly downgraded, but note the downgrade rests on absence of evidence (no clock/cert record, F19/F20/F41/F44) from a change feed that is service-scoped and provably cannot see secrets-manager/mesh-level events (F24/F45). 'Not recorded' is weaker than 'excluded'.

Rightly rejected on the strength of the independent caller-side series (F11) rather than metric self-consistency; but the underlying metric backend did return 503s (F31/F42) and the identity-namespace pipeline is down, so no claim about absolute error magnitude should be made — only about the caller-observable step.
